title: Filming New York’s brand-new subway in 1905 took three trains

cover.alt: Dark black-and-white film still: a curving arched subway tunnel, with a lit railway car on the left-hand track.
cover.credit: G. W. Bitzer, American Mutoscope & Biograph · Public domain

body: To film a ride through the tunnels, Biograph brought its own light. Cameraman Billy Bitzer’s camera sat on a platform on the front of a train that followed another train along the same track, while a specially built work car ran on the **parallel track** to light the tunnel. Shot on 21 May 1905, the film rides the Interborough line from Union Square at 14th Street to the old Grand Central Station at 42nd Street. The subway was then only seven months old.

slides.alt: Dark black-and-white film from the front of a moving subway train: in a curving arched tunnel, a lit car runs on the left-hand track, then the lit rear of the train ahead appears in the middle.
slides.caption: 21 May 1905, filmed from the front of a train: a lit car keeps pace on the left-hand track as the tunnel curves, then the train ahead comes into view.
slides.credit: G. W. Bitzer, American Mutoscope & Biograph · Public domain · excerpt

steps.label: A train runs ahead, to be filmed
The camera rides on the front of a second
A lighting car runs on the next track

events.text: Cameraman Billy Bitzer films 14th St. to 42nd St.
The Biograph company copyrights the film

slides.question: Where does the ride end?
options: At the old Grand Central Station
slides.explanation: At 42nd Street, beside the old Grand Central Station. The ride begins at Union Square on 14th Street and follows today’s East Side line.

slides.prompt: How has the Library of Congress kept one copy of this film for more than a century?
slides.answer: Printed on a roll of paper
slides.detail: It is in the Library’s Paper Print Collection: a positive print on a paper roll about 355 feet long, alongside later film copies.
